The characteristics of Mesoamerican civilization
column2: Farming surpluses let Mesoamericans build civilizations with large cities, specialized workers, social classes, monumental palaces and temples, marketplaces, schools, writing, mathematics, and accurate calendars.

column1: The land-bridge migration theory
column2: The traditional theory holds that Ice Age hunters from Asia followed megafauna across the exposed Beringia land bridge and then moved south through an ice-free corridor.

column1: The coastal boat migration theory
column2: Because glaciers may have blocked the inland route, some scholars argue that early migrants traveled in small boats down the Pacific coast.

column1: The multiple-migration theory
column2: Whole-genome evidence suggests three migrations from Siberia, with the first producing most Native Americans and later waves producing Arctic peoples and Athapaskan speakers.

column1: How the Paleo-Indians lived
column2: The Paleo-Indians lived as nomadic hunter-gatherers who followed herds of megafauna, which supplied all of their food, clothing, tools, and other material needs.

column1: Why the megafauna disappeared
column2: Post-Ice Age climate change combined with human overhunting wiped out most megafauna, forcing hunters to rely on smaller game, fishing, and gathering.

column1: How regional cultures arose after the Ice Age
column2: As receding glaciers diversified ecosystems, peoples adapted to local resources and developed distinct languages, political systems, religions, and farming and hunting patterns.

column1: Why agriculture was revolutionary
column2: Growing storable crops let people settle permanently, which allowed populations to grow, workers to specialize, social classes to form, and large cities to develop.

column1: How maize was developed
column2: Over many generations, Mesoamerican farmers repeatedly replanted the largest kernels of the wild grass teosinte until the plant became productive maize.

column1: The worldwide spread of American crops
column2: After European contact, American crops such as corn, potatoes, squash, beans, and manioc spread across Europe, Africa, and Asia and revolutionized the world's diet for better and for worse.

column1: How Indians used fire to reshape the environment
column2: Woodland Indians regularly burned underbrush, which enriched the soil, encouraged new forage, and created better conditions for the deer and other game that the Indians hunted.

column1: How Native Americans transformed their environments
column2: Native Americans reshaped their lands through vast engineering projects in central Mexico, rerouted rivers, and managed forests, disproving the romantic image of untouched nature.

column1: How Amazon peoples managed the rainforest
column2: Peoples of the Amazon encouraged the growth of trees bearing edible fruit and enriched poor soils, so much of the rainforest reflects long human management.

column1: How geography and climate shaped early North Americans
column2: Regions with abundant, reliable resources supported settled, stratified societies, while arid or harsh regions like the Great Basin and Arctic favored small, mobile bands.

column1: How the Pacific Northwest's abundance shaped its peoples
column2: Rich fisheries and forests made farming unnecessary in the Pacific Northwest, giving its peoples leisure for works of art and an elaborate social and ceremonial life.

column1: How the north-south axis limited the Americas
column2: The Americas' north-south axis created sharp climate differences that made communication and the transfer of crops and technology far harder than along Eurasia's east-west axis.

column1: Why maize spread slowly through North America
column2: Maize took thousands of years to move from Mesoamerica into the Southwest and Eastern Woodlands because each new climate required farmers to breed new varieties.

column1: Why the Americas lacked draft animals
column2: Tropical barriers kept llamas and alpacas in South America, so the civilizations of Mesoamerica had no large animals for transport, plowing, or meat.

column1: Why scarce domestic animals left Native Americans vulnerable to disease
column2: With few domesticated animals, Native Americans were never exposed to animal-borne diseases and so lacked immunities comparable to those of Eurasians.

column1: How Eurasians gained immunity to disease
column2: Eurasians who survived childhood bouts of livestock-borne diseases such as smallpox and measles gained immunity, so Europeans carried diseases that their own adults resisted.

column1: The catastrophe after European contact
column2: In the decades after contact, Eurasian diseases combined with warfare, hunger, and displacement to kill Native Americans by the millions.

column1: The significance of the Clovis discoveries
column2: The Clovis and Folsom finds, confirmed by radiocarbon dating, first proved that humans lived in Ice Age America and established the first accepted chronology of American settlement.

column1: How the Olmec ball game resembled modern games
column2: Like modern sports, the Olmec ball game featured teams, a rubber ball, a marked court, spectators, and athletic stars, and the stone-ring goal recalls a basketball hoop.

column1: How the Olmec ball game differed from modern games
column2: Players struck the heavy rubber ball only with their hips, buttocks, or knees, and games carried religious meaning that could end in the sacrifice of losers.

column1: The myth of the Moundbuilders
column2: Many later white Americans wrongly credited the eastern mounds to a vanished outside race, a prejudice that denied Native peoples credit for their own monumental achievements.

column1: The decline and rebuilding of American societies before contact
column2: After many American cultures declined, the most successful new societies arose in the Caribbean and central Mexico, and both were deeply stratified.
